title: Optional groups, repeats and backreferences
summary: Group.Success for a group that may not take part, Group.Captures for a group that repeats, and backreferences that match the same text again: doubled words and matching quotes.

steps.title: A group that did not take part
body: Put `?` after a group and it becomes optional: `(?<min>[0-9]+)m(?:(?<sec>[0-9]+)s)?` matches `5m` and `5m30s`.
When the optional part is missing, the match still succeeds, but the group did not take part.
```csharp fragment
var sec = m.Groups["sec"];
int seconds = sec.Success ? int.Parse(sec.Value) : 0;
- `Group.Success` tells you whether that group matched. Its `Value` is then `""`.
- Always test `Success` on an optional group. `int.Parse("")` throws, and an empty string written to a
database looks like real data.
- A typo in a name does not throw: `m.Groups["secs"]` returns a group that never succeeds. A test that covers the
optional part catches it, so write one for every group your code reads.

steps.explain: The optional seconds group did not take part, so it reports `Success == false` and an empty value. A group name that does not exist also gives an unsuccessful group, with no exception: a typo fails silently.

steps.title: A host with an optional port
prompt: Connection settings hold `host` or `host:port`. Match the whole string, with the host (letters, digits, `_`, `.`
and `-`) in a group named `host` and the port (digits) in a group named `port`. When there is no port, the
`port` group must not take part, so the colon belongs inside the optional part.
hints: Wrap the colon and the port together in a non-capturing group, and make that group optional with `?`.
steps.explain: `(?::(?<port>[0-9]+))?` is optional as a unit, so `db01:` is rejected and a missing port leaves `port` unmatched. In code, `Success` decides between the given port and the default 5432.

steps.title: A repeated group keeps only its last value
body: When a group repeats, `Value` holds only the **last** repetition. In `tags=api,prod,eu` with
`tags=(?:(?<t>\w+),?)+`, `Groups["t"].Value` is `eu`.
Most engines (JavaScript, Python, PCRE) throw the earlier repetitions away. **.NET keeps them** in `Group.Captures`:
```csharp fragment
foreach (Capture c in m.Groups["t"].Captures)
Console.WriteLine(c.Value);    // api, prod, eu
That lets one pattern both validate a list and return its items. Elsewhere, the usual way is two steps: match
the list, then split it or run a second `Matches` over it. That is still the clearer choice when the items
themselves are complex.

steps.explain: `Value` is the last repetition. `Captures` holds every repetition, in order, so the list survives.

steps.title: Backreferences: the same text again
body: `\1` inside a pattern matches **the same text** group 1 just matched, not the same pattern. `\k<name>` does the
same for a named group.
- Doubled words in docs and commit messages: `\b(\w+)\s+\1\b` finds `the the`.
- Matching quotes: `(["'])(.*?)\1` closes with the quote it opened with, so `"O'Brien"` is read whole.
Turn on the step debugger below. Watch the engine capture `the`, then try to match exactly `the` again. On `the theme`
the backreference matches, but `\b` fails before the `m`, so there is no match there.

text: Check the the config and and restart.

steps.title: Find doubled words
prompt: Find every doubled word: a word, whitespace, and the same word again, as whole words. `the theme` is not a
doubled word, and neither is `is` inside `this is`.

all.input: it is is fine and and done

hints: Capture a word with `(\w+)`, then match whitespace and `\1`.
steps.explain: `\1` repeats the text, so `is is` matches and `is this` does not. `\s+` also crosses a line break, which is exactly where doubled words hide in prose.

steps.title: A value in matching quotes
prompt: Config values may be quoted with `"` or `'`. Find a quoted value and capture what is inside the quotes in a group
named `v`. The closing quote must be the **same** kind as the opening one, so `"O'Brien"` gives `O'Brien`.
Name the quote group too (`q`) and close it with `\k<q>`, or use a numbered group and its backreference.
hints: `["'].*?["']` stops at the first quote of either kind, so it reads `O`. The closing quote must repeat the opening one.
steps.explain: The backreference closes with the quote that opened, so double quotes inside single quotes are kept. Escaped quotes (`\"`) need more than this pattern. For real config formats (JSON, YAML, CSV), use a parser; use this for quick searches and simple formats.

steps.prompt: Match each piece of .NET syntax to what it does.
pairs: match again the text group 1 matched
match again the text the group named q matched
every repetition of a repeated group
steps.explain: Inside the pattern, a group is referred to with a backslash (`\1`, `\k<q>`). In a .NET replacement it is `$1` or `${q}`.

steps.title: A doubled-word linter
prompt: The docs team wants a check in CI that flags doubled words. Write `List<string> DoubledWords(string text)` that
returns the doubled word of each occurrence, in order, **ignoring case**: `The the` counts and returns `The`
| `The the cat sat sat on the mat.` | `["The", "sat"]` |
Use one `Regex` with a backreference and `RegexOptions.IgnoreCase` (backreferences follow that option too).
template: Dojo.Eq("The the and sat sat", new List<string> { "The", "sat" }, DoubledWords("The the cat sat sat on the mat."));
Dojo.Eq("a doubled word across a line break", new List<string> { "the" }, DoubledWords("Paris in the\nthe spring"));
Dojo.Eq("the theme is not doubled", new List<string>(), DoubledWords("the theme park"));
Dojo.Eq("is inside this is not doubled", new List<string>(), DoubledWords("this is fine"));
hints: Add `m.Groups[1].Value` (or the named group) for each match.
